sources_considered.why: Describes the demand: 'any lawful use' and removal of the autonomous-weapons safeguard.
Pentagon statement on its human-in-the-loop policy for nuclear weapons.

evidence_items.locator: paragraph beginning 'The Department of War has stated'

receipt.public_excerpt: The Department of War has stated they will only contract with AI companies who accede to “any lawful use” and remove safeguards in the cases mentioned above.

evidence_items.explanation: The demand was bounded only by 'lawful use', and the fully autonomous weapons safeguard was to be removed. This is consistent with Marcus's inference, but it is not explicit about nuclear weapons.

receipt.public_excerpt: “It remains the Department’s policy that there is a human in the loop on all decisions on whether to employ nuclear weapons,” a senior defense official said.

evidence_items.explanation: Pentagon policy kept a human in the loop for nuclear employment, which cuts against the inference. But a policy is not a contract term, and it can change.

evidence_items.locator: section 'United States', quotation of Sec. 1638 FY2025 NDAA

receipt.public_excerpt: “It is the policy of the United States that the use of artificial intelligence efforts should not compromise … the principle of requiring positive human actions in execution of decisions by the President with respect to the employment of nuclear weapons.”

evidence_items.explanation: Statute declares a US policy of human action in nuclear employment decisions. Whether this binds 'lawful use' is unclear, since it is a policy statement rather than a prohibition.

unresolved_gaps: The proposed contract language is not public, so it is unknown whether it contained any nuclear carve-out.
It is unsettled whether Sec. 1638 and Pentagon policy would make AI-controlled nuclear employment 'unlawful' under an 'any lawful use' clause.
